records.title: Urashima Taro and the Dragon Palace
records.summary: A humble fisherman named Urashima Taro rescues a small sea turtle from torment by village children on the beach. In gratitude, the turtle transports Taro beneath the waves to the undersea Dragon Palace of Ryugu-jo, where the radiant Dragon Princess Otohime rewards him with opulent banquets. After what feels like three joyful days, Taro longs to see his elderly mother. Otohime presents him with a jeweled lacquer box (tamatebako), bidding him never to open it. Returning to his coastal village, he finds three hundred years have passed and his home is gone. Despairing, he unseals the box, releasing a plume of white smoke that turns him into a decrepit, dying centenarian.
alternate_names: The Fisherman and the Sea Kingdom
records.historical_period: Nara / Heian Period (recorded c. 720 CE Nihon Shoki and Tango no Kuni Fudoki)
records.region_or_community: Tango Province, Kyoto Prefecture coastal region

records.title: Momotaro the Peach Boy
records.summary: Discovered inside a gigantic peach floating down a mountain stream by an elderly, childless washerwoman, Momotaro grows rapidly into a youth of formidable strength and virtuous courage. When plundering ogres (oni) from the fortress island of Onigashima devastate the surrounding provinces, Momotaro sets out to subdue them, equipped with millet dumplings (kibi dango) prepared by his adoptive mother. En route, he enlists a talking spotted dog, a clever pheasant, and a nimble monkey as sworn allies. In a coordinated assault on Onigashima, the companions breach the iron fortress, force the oni chief to surrender, and return the stolen treasures to the realm.
records.historical_period: Edo Period (popularized in Kusazōshi woodblock prints c. 17th Century)

records.title: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter and Princess Kaguya
records.summary: Considered Japan's oldest prose narrative, an impoverished bamboo cutter named Taketori no Okina splits open a glowing stalk of bamboo in the forest and discovers a miniature maiden no taller than a thumb. Reared by the cutter and his wife, she blossoms into Princess Kaguya, a woman of unearthly radiance. Five noble suitors and the Emperor of Japan vie for her hand, but she sets each nobleman an impossible quest: retrieving the stone begging bowl of Buddha, a jewel from a dragon's neck, a fire-rat robe, and a swallow's cowrie shell. Weeping, she reveals she is a celestial exile from the Moon (Tsuki no Miyako) and must return home aboard a moon chariot.
records.historical_period: Early Heian Period (c. 9th to 10th Century CE)

records.title: Yuki-onna the Snow Maiden
records.summary: During a blizzard in Musashi province, two woodcutters, old Mosaku and young Minokichi, seek shelter in a dilapidated ferryman's hut. In the night, Minokichi awakens to see a breathtakingly pale maiden with white kimono and icy breath freezing old Mosaku to death. Sparing Minokichi because of his youth, the Yuki-onna extracts a solemn vow: he must never speak of her to any soul. Years later, Minokichi marries a delicate beauty named Oyuki who never seems to age. One evening while she sews by candlelight, he reminisces about the mountain spirit. Oyuki transforms back into the wraith, weeping that he broke his oath, but spares his life for their children before vanishing into snow flurries.
records.historical_period: Edo Period oral tradition (recorded 1904 by Lafcadio Hearn in Kwaidan)
records.region_or_community: Musashi and Tohoku mountainous snow country

records.title: Tamamo-no-Mae and the Killing Stone
records.summary: During the reign of Retired Emperor Toba in the twelfth century, a peerless courtesan named Tamamo-no-Mae captivates the Imperial Court with her brilliance and beauty, while her body naturally radiates sweet perfume. When the sovereign sickens mysteriously, the master onmyōji astrologer Abe no Yasunari uses holy mirrors to divine her true nature: a malevolent golden-haired, nine-tailed kitsune (kyūbi no kitsune). Exposed, the demon fox flees across the northern moorlands of Nasu, where she is slain by royal archers. Her vengeful spirit possesses a boulder that emits toxic volcanic gases, killing any bird or creature touching it, known as the Sesshō-seki.
records.historical_period: Kamakura / Muromachi Period (originating c. 12th Century legend cycle)

records.title: The Crane Wife: Tsuru no Ongaeshi
records.summary: A solitary peasant rescues an injured crane caught in an iron hunter's snare, gently dressing its wing and freeing it into the winter sky. Soon after, a modest young woman arrives at his cottage during a storm, asking to become his bride. To lift the household out of poverty, she weaves dazzling brocades on her loom under the strict condition that he never enter her weaving room. Spurred by greed and curiosity when town merchants pay huge sums, the peasant peeks through the screen and recoils in sorrow: a featherless crane is plucking its own down feathers to weave into thread. Unmasked, the weeping bird takes wing into the clouds, never to return.
records.historical_period: Edo Period folk narrative (widespread rural otogi-banashi)

records.title: Kintaro the Golden Boy of Mount Ashigara
records.summary: Raised deep in the dense mountain forests of Mount Ashigara by Yama-uba, the mountain crone, Kintaro is a child of supernatural strength clad only in a red bib embroidered with the character for 'gold' (kin). He befriends forest animals, wrestles bears in clearing rings, and uses a woodcutter's axe to fell giant pine trees for bridges. His fame reaches the mighty samurai commander Minamoto no Yorimitsu, who recruits him as one of his elite Four Heavenly Kings (Shitennō) under the adult name Sakata no Kintoki, where he helps subjugate the demon Shuten-dōji on Mount Oe.
records.historical_period: Heian Period setting (c. 10th Century, popularized in Edo Kabuki)

records.title: The Teakettle of Good Fortune (Bunbuku Chagama)
records.summary: A destitute junk merchant rescues an injured tanuki (Japanese raccoon dog) from a trap. In gratitude, the mischievous shapeshifter transforms itself into a fine bronze tea kettle, which the merchant sells to the head priest of Morin-ji temple. When the temple acolyte places the kettle over a roaring charcoal fire to boil ceremonial water, the kettle sprouts fur, four stubby legs, and a bushy tail, leaping around the hall in agony. Rescued once more by the junk dealer, the tanuki puts on humorous high-wire acrobatic shows across the province, making both of them wealthy before retiring peacefully at the temple.
records.historical_period: Muromachi to Edo Period (tradition anchored at Morin-ji temple c. 14th Century)

records.title: Issun-boshi the One-Inch Boy
records.summary: Born to an elderly couple who prayed for a child even if he were only as tall as a fingertip, Issun-boshi sets out for the imperial capital of Kyoto armed with a sewing needle for a sword, a soup bowl for a boat, and a chopstick for an oar. In Kyoto, he gains employment guarding the Chancellor's daughter. While escorting the princess to Kiyomizu-dera temple, they are ambushed by two towering oni. Swallowed whole by an ogre, Issun-boshi stabs the monster's stomach from the inside until the beast retches him up and flees in terror, dropping the magical mallet of wishes (uchide no kozuchi). Waving the treasure, the princess grows him into a handsome full-sized samurai.
records.region_or_community: Kyoto and Naniwa (Osaka) water transit routes

records.title: The Tongue-Cut Sparrow: Shita-kiri Suzume
records.summary: A kind-hearted old woodsman befriends an injured sparrow, tending it gently at his home. One day while he is gathering firewood, the woodsman's greedy, quarrelsome wife snips off the sparrow's tongue with sewing shears as punishment for eating her starch paste, driving the bird into the forest. Searching the bamboo groves, the grieving man finds the sparrow's hidden village, where the birds greet him with festive hospitality and offer a choice between a heavy or light wicker basket. Choosing the light basket out of modesty, he discovers it filled with gold coins. His envious wife rushes to the forest, snatches the heavy basket, and opens it, only to be devoured by demons and venomous serpents.
alternate_names: The Sparrow with the Slit Tongue
records.historical_period: Edo Period (popularized in Edo educational primers)
